modalities.name: Long Settle Imagery
modalities.tagline: Deep calm first, then one slow scene of being cared for.
modalities.whatItIs: Long Settle Imagery is a new, untested idea that pushes ideal parent imagery (picturing yourself as a child cared for by invented, ideal parents) further toward calm and absorption than the original method. A trained therapist spends most of a long session helping you settle deeply, then guides one slow, unchanging scene of being cared for, instead of exploring or talking with different sides of yourself.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that care might sink in more fully when you are deeply settled and simply receiving, so the session spends its time on settling and receiving rather than on talking or exploring.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 90-minute session, the therapist guides about 40 minutes of slow settling through the breath, a body scan and a gradual quieting of thought. Then comes a single, carefully paced scene in which ideal parents protect, soothe and delight in the child you imagine being, followed by a slow return and a short talk about what stayed with you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with lasting insecurity in close relationships who find that talk-heavy therapy keeps them in their heads, and who settle well with guided relaxation.
modalities.cautions: Deep calm can lower defenses and blur imagination with memory, so a licensed clinician trained in trauma care leads every session and keeps the scene clearly imagined, and people prone to dissociation should avoid long relaxation inductions. The practice draws only on memories you already have, treats any image or feeling that surfaces as imagination rather than evidence of what happened, is never used to uncover forgotten events, and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Long Settle Imagery. A therapist spends most of the session helping you sink into deep calm, then guides one slow scene of being cared for by imagined ideal parents. For people whose minds stay busy in talk therapy. Untested, so go gently.

modalities.name: The Wordless Cradle
modalities.tagline: Imagined care from the time before you had words.
modalities.whatItIs: The Wordless Cradle is a proposed practice that takes ideal parent imagery, in which you picture yourself as a child cared for by invented ideal parents, back to the earliest part of life, before language. Instead of scenes with conversations, you imagine being a baby who is held, rocked, fed and kept warm by ideal parents, and you mostly notice how that care feels in your body.
modalities.coreIdea: The first lessons about whether care can be relied on are learned before words, so this practice works with wordless, bodily images of being held rather than with talk, agendas or structured steps.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lying or reclining under a blanket, you follow a therapist's slow, sparse descriptions of being held close, rocked and warmed, with long quiet pauses in between. There is no goal to reach and little talking; at the end you describe in a few words what you felt, and the therapist checks how settled you are before you leave.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who sense that their insecurity runs deeper than any memory and who find that words get in the way of feeling cared for.
modalities.cautions: Imagining infancy can bring up strong, hard-to-name longing or grief and feel very exposing, so it belongs only in ongoing therapy led by a licensed therapist with training in trauma care and attachment work, at a slow pace. The scenes are pure invention that leans on no memory beyond those you already hold, sensations that come are not evidence of anything that happened in infancy, it must never be used to 'recover' forgotten events, and it does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: An idea: The Wordless Cradle. With a trained therapist you imagine being a baby who is held, rocked and kept warm by ideal parents, with almost no talking. For adults whose insecurity feels older than words. Untested, and only with a trauma-aware guide.

modalities.name: One Age at a Time
modalities.tagline: Ideal parent imagery as a planned journey through childhood.
modalities.whatItIs: One Age at a Time is a new, untested idea that turns ideal parent imagery into a planned journey through childhood, from toddler to teenager. Each block of sessions imagines ideal parents meeting the needs of one age, such as a five-year-old's fears at night or a teenager's need for both freedom and limits.
modalities.coreIdea: Children need different kinds of care at different ages, so this practice offers imagined care stage by stage, rather than as one general scene, and moves on only when an age feels settled.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a trained therapist first choose about six ages to visit, from around two to sixteen. Over several weekly sessions per age, the therapist guides scenes of ideal parents caring for you at that age, and you move on to the next age only when the current one feels settled to you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who notice that their struggles in relationships feel tied to particular stages, such as early school years or adolescence, and who like a clear long-term plan.
modalities.cautions: Moving through the years can stir up memories of what really happened at each age, so the lead must be a licensed clinician trained in trauma care who keeps imagined scenes apart from memories. It stays with what you already remember, takes no image or feeling as proof of past events, is never a way to unearth forgotten years, and as long-term work with no evidence behind it, it should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: One Age at a Time. Ideal parent imagery as a planned journey through childhood, one age per block of sessions, from toddler to teen, each with the care that age needed. For adults who feel stuck at one stage. Untested; needs a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Tucked In Imagery
modalities.tagline: Comfort only: an imagined bedtime with parents who stay.
modalities.whatItIs: Tucked In Imagery is a gentle, untested variation on ideal parent imagery that stays entirely on soothing, with no searching for what hurts or why. Each session imagines one ordinary bedtime: ideal parents settling the child you picture being, staying close and leaving a light on, until the scene ends in safe, sleepy calm.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people may need to feel soothed many times before they can safely look at anything painful, so this practice offers comfort only and never goes digging.
modalities.whatYouDo: You lie or recline in a dim, quiet room while the therapist guides a 20-minute bedtime scene: a bath, a story, a tucking in, and parents who stay until you feel drowsy. Afterwards you rest for a few minutes, sit up slowly and talk briefly about how calm you feel, rather than about the past.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel on edge most of the time, find bedtime or being alone at night hard, and want a gentle way in before any deeper work.
modalities.cautions: Even soothing scenes can awaken grief for the care you missed, so the work happens only within therapy led by a licensed, trauma-trained clinician who knows attachment work, alongside any care you already receive, and deep relaxation can leave you drowsy, so wait a few minutes before driving. The bedtime scene is invented: it calls on no memory you do not already have, feelings it stirs are not evidence about your real childhood, and it is never used to search for forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: What if therapy began with being tucked in? Tucked In Imagery is an untested idea: a therapist guides a calm bedtime scene where ideal parents settle the child you picture being, with no digging into the past. For people who rarely feel safe enough to rest.

modalities.name: Overheard Kindness
modalities.tagline: Imagining ideal parents speaking warmly about you, out of earshot.
modalities.whatItIs: Overheard Kindness is a proposed variation on ideal parent imagery, in which you picture yourself as a child cared for by invented ideal parents, that works only through words, with no body work at all. Instead of being spoken to directly, the child you picture being overhears the ideal parents talking warmly about them in the next room, when they think no one is listening.
modalities.coreIdea: Praise said to your face can feel like politeness, but kind words overheard are harder to dismiss, so the practice delivers care as something the parents say when they have nothing to gain.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly sessions, a therapist guides you to picture yourself as a child in bed or on the stairs, hearing the ideal parents talk about your day, what they noticed and what they love about you. The therapist voices both parents in slow, ordinary sentences, and afterwards you note which overheard line stayed with you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who brush off compliments, suspect kindness has a motive, or grew up overhearing criticism rather than warmth.
modalities.cautions: Overhearing scenes can echo real memories of arguments or harsh talk, so a licensed clinician trained in trauma care leads and keeps the scenes clearly invented. If an old memory does come up, it is one you already had and is met gently as it is, nothing heard in the imagery is taken as evidence of what was said at home, and the practice is never used to dig for forgotten events; it is untested and should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Overheard Kindness. In guided imagery, the child you once were overhears imagined ideal parents in the next room talking warmly about you when they think you can't hear. For people who brush off compliments. Untested; with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Shared Project
modalities.tagline: Building something with imagined ideal parents over many sessions.
modalities.whatItIs: The Shared Project is an experimental extension of ideal parent imagery, in which you picture yourself as a child cared for by invented ideal parents, built around one long joint project, such as a treehouse, a garden or a model boat. Instead of waiting to see what feeling arises, the therapist plans each scene as the next stage of the project, so care comes through working side by side on something that grows.
modalities.coreIdea: Children learn that they are capable and worth investing in partly by making things with an adult who is patient and pleased with them, so this practice gives that experience a continuing shape across sessions.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and the therapist choose the project and plan its stages in advance, from drawing the plan to the finishing touches. Each session the therapist guides one stage, in which the ideal parents work alongside the imagined child, let mistakes happen without fuss and show how pleased they are with each small piece, and you end by noting what was built today.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who were rarely helped or encouraged to make things as children, or who feel nothing they do is ever good enough.
modalities.cautions: Scenes of patient help can bring up grief for what was missing, so the sessions are led by a licensed therapist with training in trauma and attachment care who keeps the scenes clearly invented. The project uses only memories you already carry, counts no image or feeling as proof of how things really were, never goes looking for forgotten events, and is untested, so it does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Concept: The Shared Project. Guided imagery where invented ideal parents build a treehouse or garden with you as a child, one stage per session, pleased with every small piece. For people who never felt good enough. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Kind Limits Imagery
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who set firm, warm limits and stay kind.
modalities.whatItIs: Kind Limits Imagery is a speculative idea that pushes ideal parent imagery toward firm structure, far from open, unfolding presence. The scenes center on ideal parents setting clear, predictable limits, such as bedtime, no hitting or homework before games, and staying warm and steady when the imagined child protests.
modalities.coreIdea: Secure children learn that limits and love can come together, so experiencing kind, consistent limits in imagination might loosen a belief that rules mean rejection or that love means no limits.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trained therapist, you choose a few everyday limits a child might meet, and the therapist guides scripted scenes in which the ideal parents state each limit simply, hold it calmly when the imagined child is angry or sad, and then offer comfort. You note how it feels to be held to a limit without being shamed, and the same limits repeat across sessions.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who grew up with either harsh rules or no rules at all, and who feel crushed or lost when others set boundaries.
modalities.cautions: Limit scenes can echo memories of harsh or frightening discipline, so a licensed clinician with trauma training leads, keeping every limit gentle and the scenes clearly invented. Any memory that comes up is one you already had, forgotten events are never something to dig for, and feelings the scenes stir are not evidence of how you were really disciplined; there is no evidence for the practice yet, so it should not replace well-tested care.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Kind Limits Imagery. Guided imagery where invented ideal parents set clear limits, like bedtime or no hitting, and stay warm and steady when the child inside you protests. For people who learned rules mean rejection. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Twin Guide Intensive
modalities.tagline: A few planned days of imagery, with two practitioners present.
modalities.whatItIs: Twin Guide Intensive is an untested concept that runs ideal parent imagery as a concentrated block of sessions over a few days, with every minute planned. Two trained practitioners work together: one voices and guides the imagery while the other watches your breathing and posture, tracks your comfort and calls pauses.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentrated, carefully planned time with imagined care might build momentum that weekly sessions lose between visits, and a second practitioner makes that intensity safer to hold.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over three to five days you have two or three planned sessions a day, each with a short settling, a scripted scene and a structured debrief, plus rest breaks and meals at set times. Both practitioners meet you before and after the block to agree on stop signals and to plan follow-up with your regular therapist.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults already in therapy for attachment difficulties who feel that weekly sessions lose momentum and who can take a few days away from daily demands.
modalities.cautions: Intensive formats can stir up a lot quickly, so it is only for people screened as stable enough, never during a crisis, and the lead practitioner must be a licensed clinician skilled in trauma care, with a second experienced practitioner, clear stop signals and planned aftercare. The scenes rely only on memories you already have, nothing seen or felt during the days counts as evidence of past events, the intensive is never used to uncover forgotten ones, and it does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Twin Guide Intensive. A few days of planned ideal parent imagery, where one practitioner guides the scenes and a second watches your comfort and calls pauses. For people in therapy who feel weekly sessions lose momentum. Not for a crisis.

modalities.name: Known in Detail
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who know the small, particular facts of you.
modalities.whatItIs: Known in Detail is an untested idea that turns ideal parent imagery away from general, all-embracing goodwill and toward particular knowledge. The imagined ideal parents know the imagined child in fine detail, details you and the therapist invent together: the stuffed toy it sleeps with, the joke that makes it laugh, the food it refuses, the worry it has not mentioned yet.
modalities.coreIdea: Kindness wished to everyone can feel impersonal, so this practice builds the experience of being cared for by someone who knows you specifically and remembers.
modalities.whatYouDo: In early sessions, you and a trained therapist invent the small details of the imagined child together, such as a favorite toy, a silly song and a food it refuses, choosing them freely rather than taking them from your real childhood. Later sessions guide scenes in which the ideal parents notice and use those details, remembering a favorite song on a hard day or knowing what you need before you ask.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel interchangeable, unseen in their particulars, or loved only in general terms.
modalities.cautions: Even invented details can call up real memories, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist who knows attachment and trauma work and keeps the imagined child and parents clearly separate from real ones. It is untested and cannot stand in for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Known in Detail. Guided imagery where ideal parents know every small, invented fact about the imagined child: its favorite toy, the joke that makes it laugh. For people who feel loved only in general terms. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Proudly Introduced
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who introduce you, by name, with pride.
modalities.whatItIs: Proudly Introduced is a hypothetical practice that turns ideal parent imagery toward being claimed in public. Where insight meditation loosens the sense of a fixed self, this practice builds one: the imagined ideal parents introduce you as a child, by name, to relatives, neighbors and teachers, with obvious pride in who you are.
modalities.coreIdea: A secure sense of self grows partly from being claimed and named by people who are glad you are theirs, so this practice gives that experience directly in imagination.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist guides scenes in which the ideal parents walk into a school, a family party or a neighbor's kitchen and introduce you with a sentence or two about what makes you you, such as 'this is our daughter, she knows every bird in the garden'. You notice what it is like to be named and placed among people, and the imagined gatherings vary from session to session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel like outsiders in families or groups, or who never felt anyone was proud to call them their own.
modalities.cautions: Scenes of belonging can stir up painful feelings about real family occasions, so a licensed therapist with trauma training leads and keeps the gatherings clearly invented. It draws on no memory beyond what you already recall, treats the feelings it brings as reactions rather than proof of how your family saw you, never sets out to uncover forgotten events, and as an unproven idea it is no replacement for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Proudly Introduced. Guided imagery where invented ideal parents introduce you as a child, by name, to relatives and teachers, plainly proud you are theirs. For people who never felt anyone was proud to call them their own. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: All Afternoon for You
modalities.tagline: Imagined time with parents who have nowhere else to be.
modalities.whatItIs: All Afternoon for You is a speculative idea that pushes ideal parent imagery toward complete rest and open time, the opposite of anything timed or intense. Each session imagines a long, lazy afternoon in which ideal parents have nowhere else to be, ask nothing of the imagined child and simply enjoy the time together.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people learned that attention had to be earned or squeezed in, so this practice offers imagined time with no clock, no tasks and nothing to prove.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting or lying comfortably, you follow a therapist's loose, slow guidance into a scene such as a quiet afternoon at home, with fewer set steps than usual and plenty of silence. You are free to let the scene drift, and the session ends with a few minutes of noticing how it feels to have had someone's time without asking for it.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who always feel rushed, feel like a burden on other people's time, or believe they must perform to be wanted.
modalities.cautions: Loosely guided imagery can drift toward painful memories or leave you drowsy or spacey, so a licensed clinician schooled in trauma care leads and checks in often. If the scene drifts toward a real memory, it is one you already had and the clinician gently steers back, since images that surface are not evidence of what happened and the practice is never used to bring forgotten events to light; as an untested idea it sits alongside well-tested treatments rather than replacing them.
modalities.tweet: What if someone had nowhere else to be but with you? All Afternoon for You is guided imagery where ideal parents ask nothing, rush nowhere and simply enjoy your company. For anyone who feels like a burden on others' time. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Held in Solitude
modalities.tagline: Learning to be alone while still feeling cared for.
modalities.whatItIs: Held in Solitude is a thought experiment that uses ideal parent imagery to practice being alone without feeling abandoned. After guided sessions that build a scene of ideal parents, you spend stretches of quiet time by yourself, sensing that the imagined care stays with you even when no one is there.
modalities.coreIdea: A secure child can play happily alone because a caring presence feels close inside, so this practice trains that inner company directly, in solitude rather than with other people.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session begins with a therapist guiding a short scene of ideal parents, then you sit alone in a quiet room for 20 to 40 minutes, with the therapist nearby and a simple way to call them. Afterwards you meet briefly to talk about when the inner company felt near or far, and the alone time grows slowly over the weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find being alone frightening or empty, and who fill every quiet moment with screens, noise or other people.
modalities.cautions: Time alone can bring up loneliness or old fears of abandonment, so it runs only inside therapy led by a licensed, trauma-trained clinician, with small steps, the therapist always within reach, and no solitude practice for anyone at risk of self-harm. The inner company is imagined, not remembered: it uses only memories you already have, takes no feeling in the quiet room as evidence of past events, is never a search for forgotten ones, and is no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: For people who find being alone frightening, a new idea: Held in Solitude. A therapist helps you build imagery of ideal parents, then you practice short stretches of quiet time alone, sensing the care stays with you. Untested, built up in small steps.

modalities.name: Little and Often Visits
modalities.tagline: Short, frequent scenes of care instead of long sessions.
modalities.whatItIs: Little and Often Visits proposes delivering ideal parent imagery, the practice of picturing care from invented ideal parents, in very short, frequent sessions instead of long ones. A trained therapist guides brief, tightly structured scenes of about ten minutes, several times a week, so the experience of being cared for comes back often, the way a young child is checked on through the day.
modalities.coreIdea: Secure care is built from many small, reliable moments rather than a few long ones, so in this practice frequency matters more than length or stamina.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three or four times a week you meet a therapist, in person or by video, for a 15-minute slot: a minute to settle, about ten minutes of one scripted scene and a quick check of how you feel. Scenes repeat with small variations, and once a month a longer session reviews how it is going.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find long sessions draining or hard to fit in, or whose sense of being cared for fades quickly between weekly visits.
modalities.cautions: Short slots leave little time to settle if something painful comes up, so the lead must be a licensed clinician with trauma training, with a plan for a longer follow-up when needed. The scenes call on no memories beyond the ones you already have, images in them are not evidence of how you were really cared for, they are never used to recover forgotten events, and with no evidence yet the practice should not replace well-tested care.
modalities.tweet: Little and often, the way a child is checked on all day: the idea behind Little and Often Visits. A therapist guides a ten-minute scene of imagined ideal parents several times a week. For people whose sense of care fades fast. No evidence yet.

modalities.name: Carried for a While
modalities.tagline: Imagery for practicing being helped instead of being strong.
modalities.whatItIs: Carried for a While is an untested concept that uses ideal parent imagery to practice being helped rather than being strong. The scenes picture ideal parents carrying the child, taking the heavy bags, sorting out the problem and letting the child lean on them completely, with no expectation of coping alone.
modalities.coreIdea: People who had to grow up fast may never have felt what it is like to depend on someone, so this practice makes imagined dependence, rather than effort or self-reliance, the main experience.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly sessions, a trained therapist guides slow, loosely structured scenes of being carried, looked after when ill, or having a grown-up take over a task that was too much. You notice any urge to take back control, let the imagined parents keep carrying, and end by naming one small way you might accept help this week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who are always the strong one, find it very hard to ask for help, and feel uneasy when others look after them.
modalities.cautions: Letting yourself lean, even in imagination, can bring up grief about having had to cope alone, so it belongs only within therapy led by a licensed therapist with training in trauma and attachment care. It uses only memories you already hold, treats what you feel while being carried as imagination rather than evidence about the past, never digs for forgotten events, and is an untested idea that does not stand in for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: For everyone who is always the strong one, an idea: Carried for a While. Guided imagery where ideal parents carry the load and let the child you once were lean on them completely. A way to practice being helped. Untested; needs a trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Imagined Home
modalities.tagline: Designing, then visiting, the calm household you never had.
modalities.whatItIs: The Imagined Home is a proposed extension of ideal parent imagery that builds not only the ideal parents but the whole household they keep: the rooms, the meals, the rules and the daily rhythm. Over many sessions you and a therapist design this home in detail, then spend guided time living ordinary days in it.
modalities.coreIdea: Security grows from a predictable everyday world as much as from single moments of comfort, so this practice gives that world a lasting, structured shape in imagination.
modalities.whatYouDo: Early sessions are spent describing the house with the therapist: where the child's room is, what breakfast is like, how disagreements are handled and who is home after school. Later, the therapist guides 20-minute scenes of ordinary moments there, and you return to the same rooms each week so that they become familiar.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who grew up in chaotic or unpredictable homes and who long for a sense of order, routine and belonging.
modalities.cautions: Building an ideal home can highlight what your real home lacked and bring up grief or anger, so a licensed clinician skilled in trauma care leads and keeps the imagined home clearly separate from memories. Designing it relies only on what you already remember, any feeling it stirs is not evidence about your real home, it is never used to uncover forgotten events, and since nothing is known yet about whether it helps, it should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: What if you could spend time in a calm, predictable imagined home? The Imagined Home is a new concept: with a therapist you design its rooms, meals and routines, then spend guided time there. For people who grew up in chaos. Still to be tested.

modalities.name: The Asking Hour
modalities.tagline: The questions you never asked as a child, kindly answered.
modalities.whatItIs: The Asking Hour is a hypothetical practice that turns ideal parent imagery into a two-way exchange. In the imagined scene, your imagined younger self asks the questions children often carry in silence, such as whether they are too much or why people leave, and the imagined ideal parents answer honestly and kindly.
modalities.coreIdea: Unspoken childhood questions tend to get answered by fear, so this practice gives them a chance to be asked out loud and answered with care.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before the imagery, you and a trained therapist choose one question you would have wanted to ask as a child. During a guided scene you ask it, wait and let the imagined parents' answer come, with the therapist stepping in if the answer turns harsh, and afterwards you write the answer down in a sentence or two.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who carry nagging questions about their worth or about relationships, and who like the idea of talking with imagined caregivers, not only receiving from them.
modalities.cautions: Questions like these can lead straight to painful memories, so a licensed, trauma-trained clinician leads and keeps the answers clearly imagined, kind and separate from what really happened. The imagined answer is not evidence of what your real parents thought, the work uses only memories you already have and never goes looking for forgotten ones, and it is untested, so it should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Novel idea: The Asking Hour. In guided imagery, the child you once were finally asks the big questions (am I too much? will you stay?) and imagined ideal parents answer kindly. For people still carrying those questions. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: No Need to Talk
modalities.tagline: Being cared for without having to explain or perform.
modalities.whatItIs: No Need to Talk is a new idea that removes the social effort from ideal parent imagery: you never have to explain, report or be good company. The session follows a fixed sequence, and you respond only with small agreed hand signals while imagined ideal parents care for the child in the scene.
modalities.coreIdea: For people who learned that closeness means performing, being cared for without having to speak or please anyone might be a new experience in itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the first meeting you and a trained therapist agree on the script and on three signals, such as one finger for more, two for slow down and an open hand for stop. In later sessions you sit or lie with eyes closed through a 30-minute guided scene, signaling when needed, with only a brief, optional check-in at the end.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel drained by talking about themselves, who people-please in conversation, or who find the social side of therapy exhausting.
modalities.cautions: With little talking the clinician has less to go on, so the lead must be a licensed clinician schooled in trauma care who watches closely and always honors the stop signal. The scene uses only memories you already have, nothing felt in the silence counts as evidence of what happened, it is never used to uncover forgotten events, and as an untested idea it sits alongside well-tested treatments rather than replacing them.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people worn out by talking about themselves: No Need to Talk. A therapist guides imagery of ideal parents caring for your younger self, and you answer only with hand signals. No explaining, no performing. Untested concept.

modalities.name: Same Scene, Thirty Times
modalities.tagline: One carefully written scene of care, repeated word for word.
modalities.whatItIs: Same Scene, Thirty Times is a speculative idea that pushes ideal parent imagery to the far end of structure. You and a therapist write one short scene of ideal parents caring for the imagined child, then the therapist guides that exact script, word for word, in about thirty sessions spread over several months.
modalities.coreIdea: Where open, varied experience brings surprise, secure care is partly about sameness, so this practice makes exact repetition the point: the care comes back identical every time.
modalities.whatYouDo: In the first two sessions you and the therapist draft and refine a five-minute script, choosing every word, image and pause. After that, each session opens with the script read in the same voice and pace, followed by a few minutes of rest and a short note on what felt different this time.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who grew up with unpredictable care and who find comfort in routine, ritual and knowing exactly what comes next.
modalities.cautions: Repetition can turn flat or, for some people, stir up memories of rigid or controlling homes, so a licensed therapist with trauma training leads and can pause or revise the script at any time. The script is invented and calls on no memory you do not already have, the feelings it brings are not evidence of what your childhood was like, it is never used to uncover forgotten events, and since nothing about it has been tested, keep any care you already have.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: Same Scene, Thirty Times. One short scene of ideal parents caring for you as a child, written with a therapist and then repeated word for word for months. For people who grew up with unpredictable care. Untested.

modalities.name: Mended Mistake Scenes
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who get it wrong, then make it right.
modalities.whatItIs: Mended Mistake Scenes adds something unusual to ideal parent imagery, a method of picturing care from invented ideal parents: the ideal parents sometimes get things wrong. In planned scenes they are distracted, misunderstand or snap, then notice, apologize and make it right, so your imagined younger self learns that a bond can survive mistakes.
modalities.coreIdea: Secure relationships are not perfect ones but ones where breaks get repaired, so this practice rehearses repair rather than flawless care.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist guides structured scenes in three parts: a small, clearly mild misstep by the imagined parents, a pause to notice the hurt, and a warm repair with an apology and a change of course. You rate how safe the relationship feels before and after each repair, and the misstep is always kept small and never resembles real harm.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who experience any conflict or mistake as the end of a relationship, or who cannot forgive themselves or others for small failures.
modalities.cautions: Even mild imagined missteps can echo real hurts, so the scenes stay small and a licensed clinician with trauma training leads. If a real hurt comes to mind it is one you already remember, the scenes never serve to dig up forgotten ones, and what you feel in them is not evidence of what happened in your family; it is an untested idea and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: imagery where ideal parents sometimes get it wrong, then apologize and make it right. Mended Mistake Scenes rehearses repair, not perfection. For people who fear any conflict ends a relationship. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Seen With Kind Eyes
modalities.tagline: The quiet experience of being looked at with delight.
modalities.whatItIs: Seen With Kind Eyes is an invented practice that narrows ideal parent imagery down to one silent experience: being looked at with warmth. There is no music, no story and almost no talking, and the scenes center on an imagined ideal parent's face lighting up as they see the child in the scene.
modalities.coreIdea: Much early attunement happens through faces and eyes rather than through words or sound, so this practice concentrates on the quiet experience of being seen and enjoyed.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a quiet room, a trained therapist guides a short, structured scene: you picture an ideal parent's face, their eyes finding yours and their expression softening into delight, then you stay with that image in silence for a few minutes. The scene repeats with small variations, such as being seen after a fall or after a success, and ends with a brief check-in.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel invisible, uneasy being looked at, or unsure whether anyone is glad they exist.
modalities.cautions: Being looked at, even in imagination, can feel exposing or stir up memories of cold or angry faces, so a licensed, trauma-trained clinician who knows attachment work leads and keeps it gentle. The face is imagined, the work rests only on memories you already have, any feeling it stirs is not evidence of how you were really seen, it is never used to bring back forgotten events, and as it has never been tested, keep any care you already have.
modalities.tweet: For anyone who feels invisible, an untested concept: Seen With Kind Eyes. Quiet guided imagery of an ideal parent's face lighting up when they see the small you. No music, no story, just being looked at with warmth. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Inner Siblings
modalities.tagline: Steadier sides of you looking after the younger ones.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Siblings is a proposed twist on parts work, the idea that a mind holds many sides, each with its own feelings and aims. Instead of importing imagined caregivers, it asks sides of you that are already steadier, such as a capable teenage side, to keep company with a younger side that still carries an old fear, the way an older sibling might.
modalities.coreIdea: An inner system may already hold its own helpers, so the practice looks for care among the parts themselves rather than bringing any in from outside.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist, you notice a young side of you that still holds an old fear, such as dreading being left, and ask which other sides would be willing to sit with it, checking that each feels calm and kind. In loosely guided imagery you let the helper and the young side spend time together, describing what happens without steering it, and the therapist steps in if any helper turns harsh.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find it hard to feel a calm core self, or who sense strength in some sides of themselves but not in others.
modalities.cautions: Helper sides can turn out to be protectors in disguise, and close inner relationships can stir up old family dynamics, so a licensed clinician skilled in trauma care and parts work leads, and people with dissociative conditions need specialist care instead. The work stays with memories you already have, treats the inner scenes as imagination rather than evidence of family history, is never used to dig up forgotten events, and is untested.
modalities.tweet: What if the steadier sides of you could look after the scared ones? Inner Siblings is a new idea for parts work: a capable or playful side keeps a younger, frightened side company, like an older sibling. Untested; only with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Dressed for an Old Climate
modalities.tagline: How your inner sides still dress for an old emotional climate.
modalities.whatItIs: Dressed for an Old Climate is an untested concept that looks at your inner sides as people still dressed for the emotional climate they grew up in, such as a home that felt tense, cold or unpredictable. Instead of testing or arguing with what those sides learned, sessions are open and unhurried and simply get to know the old climate as it is still felt in the body today.
modalities.coreIdea: Habits that look unreasonable now often made sense in the emotional weather of long ago, so understanding that weather, without pushing anyone to change clothes, may be enough for some sides to loosen.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist invites you to notice where an old climate is felt now, perhaps as shoulders braced against cold or a stomach ready for a storm, and to ask the side of you that holds it what the weather was like and how it learned to dress. You do not recall or reconstruct events; the work stays with the feel of the climate and the habits it taught, and nothing is asked to change.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults whose reactions feel tuned to a world they no longer live in, such as always bracing for anger or expecting no one to come.
modalities.cautions: Sensing an old emotional climate can bring strong feelings close, so a licensed therapist with training in trauma care and parts work leads, and people with dissociation or in crisis need stabilizing work first. It keeps to what you already remember, impressions of the old weather are not evidence of events, and it is never used to hunt for forgotten ones; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Dressed for an Old Climate. Parts work, with a therapist, that gets to know the sides of you still dressed for the emotional weather you grew up in, braced for cold or storms, with no forcing change. For reactions tuned to a world you've left.

modalities.name: The Inner Museum
modalities.tagline: Viewing the old beliefs of your inner sides as quiet exhibits.
modalities.whatItIs: The Inner Museum is an experimental idea that turns parts work toward history rather than present-moment goals. In imagination you and a therapist build a quiet museum where each side of you has a room displaying the beliefs and rules it learned long ago, shown as objects, such as a sign reading 'never need anyone' or a heavy coat of responsibility, rather than as scenes of what happened.
modalities.coreIdea: Viewing old learning as respectful exhibits, from the calm distance of a visitor, might let deep history be understood without being relived or reconstructed.
modalities.whatYouDo: With the therapist, you walk through the museum one room at a time, describing the objects you find and asking the side of you whose room it is what each object has meant to it. You never step into a past scene, only look at the displays from the doorway, and each visit ends by closing the room gently and noting what you learned.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who want to understand where their reactions come from and who prefer some distance from painful material.
modalities.cautions: Exhibits can still stir up painful feelings, so the lead must be a licensed clinician schooled in trauma care and parts work, who stops if the distance breaks down. Every object is a symbol built from memories you already have, never evidence of events, and the museum is never used to retrieve forgotten ones; it is untested and not a stand-in for tested treatments for trauma.
modalities.tweet: Concept: The Inner Museum. With a therapist, you imagine a museum where each side of you displays the old beliefs it learned as objects, like a sign saying 'never need anyone', seen from the doorway. For people who want distance from old patterns. Untested.

modalities.name: Skill Without the Burden
modalities.tagline: Keeping what old hardship taught you while setting its pain aside.
modalities.whatItIs: Skill Without the Burden is a speculative form of parts work built on a simple observation: sides of you shaped by old hardship often carry a real skill along with the pain, such as reading moods quickly or coping alone. Rather than dissolving the old learning, calm and unhurried sessions carefully separate the skill from the burden so the skill can be kept.
modalities.coreIdea: Parts may hold on to old pain because they fear losing what it taught them, so honoring and keeping the skill might let the burden feel safer to set down later.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist helps you find a side of you that formed under pressure and name, together with it, the skill it developed and the heavy belief that came with it, such as sharp attention to moods and the belief 'I am only safe if everyone is happy'. You notice in the body how each feels, picture the skill in your hands and the belief in a box beside you, and leave both where they are until the side is ready to decide.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who fear that letting go of old patterns would cost them strengths they rely on, such as vigilance, independence or tirelessness.
modalities.cautions: Looking at what old hardship taught can bring that hardship close, so a licensed, trauma-trained clinician experienced in parts work leads. The work stays with the skill and the belief as they are today, using only memories you already have, treating any picture of how they formed as impression rather than evidence, and never searching for forgotten events; as an untested idea it sits alongside well-tested treatments rather than replacing them.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Skill Without the Burden. Parts work that separates what old hardship taught you, like reading moods fast, from the painful belief that came with it, so the skill stays. For people afraid change would cost their strengths. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: One Belief, Many Carriers
modalities.tagline: Following one old belief through every side of you that carries it.
modalities.whatItIs: One Belief, Many Carriers is a prototype idea that organizes parts work around a single long-held belief instead of a single part. Working entirely in words, you and a therapist follow one old belief, such as 'I am too much', through each side of you that carries it, since the critic may say it harshly, the pleaser may act it out and a young side may simply feel it.
modalities.coreIdea: An old belief can survive by being spread across many sides at once, so seeing all its carriers together might show how it keeps itself going.
modalities.whatYouDo: In talk-based sessions, the therapist helps you state the belief in its exact old words and then asks, one side at a time, how each part of you holds, says or obeys it. You write the carriers and their versions on one page, and later sessions return to whichever carrier seems most ready to talk about why it took the belief on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who keep meeting the same painful belief in different disguises, at work, in love and in their own heads.
modalities.cautions: Spending time with a core belief can stir up shame and old pain, so a licensed clinician with trauma training and parts experience leads. The work stays with the belief, works only from memories you already hold, treats any sense of where it came from as impression rather than evidence, and is never used to search for forgotten events; it is untested and cannot stand in for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Idea: One Belief, Many Carriers. Parts work with a therapist, organized around one old belief, like 'I am too much', followed through every side of you that carries it: the critic says it, the pleaser acts it out. For one belief in many disguises. Untested.

modalities.name: Where the Old Dangers Are
modalities.tagline: Charting where your inner sides learned that danger lies.
modalities.whatItIs: Where the Old Dangers Are is a hypothetical practice in which a therapist leads you, step by step, in drawing up the danger map each side of you learned long ago: the feelings and situations it was taught to avoid, such as closeness, anger, success or being noticed. Instead of waiting quietly for a felt sense to form, the work is explicit and plainly named, one danger zone at a time.
modalities.coreIdea: Many sides of us still steer by a map of danger drawn in early life, so making that map visible might let a side decide, zone by zone, whether a border still needs guarding.
modalities.whatYouDo: The therapist asks a protective side of you to name the zones it keeps you out of and what it believes would happen there, and you sketch these on a simple imagined map, without going into the events that drew them. Once a zone is clear, you ask the side whether any border could move a little, and you check back on that border in later sessions.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who steer around whole areas of life, such as intimacy, conflict or ambition, without quite knowing why.
modalities.cautions: Naming old dangers can make them feel close again, so a licensed therapist with trauma training and parts experience leads, and no border moves before the side guarding it agrees. The map is drawn from memories you already have, a zone's felt danger is not evidence of what happened there, it is never used to search out forgotten events, and it is untested.
modalities.tweet: Steer around closeness, conflict or success without knowing why? Where the Old Dangers Are is a new idea: with a therapist, map the danger zones each side of you learned long ago and ask whether any border can move. Untested so far.

modalities.name: Inner Ambassadors
modalities.tagline: Sides of you posted long ago to handle particular people.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Ambassadors is an untested concept that sees some sides of you as ambassadors, each first posted long ago to one particular person, such as a harsh parent or an angry sibling, and since then sent out to handle everyone who seems like that person: authority figures, angry people or anyone who seems to need care. The structured process works on that old spread directly, showing the ambassador, one real person at a time, that it learned its job with one person and that everyone else is a separate country with a file of their own.
modalities.coreIdea: A lesson learned with one important person in childhood often spreads to everyone who resembles them, so letting the ambassador see, person by person, how each real person differs from the one it was first posted to might shrink the old lesson back to where it was learned.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist you find the side that takes over around, say, managers, and ask it who it was first posted to and what it learned there to expect, using only memories you already have. Before a meeting with a real manager you brief it in a few plain facts on how this person differs from that first posting, and afterwards it reports what it noticed and which fact surprised it. Over several encounters you keep a short dossier on each real person, and in session you lay the dossiers beside the first posting so the ambassador can feel how far each person is from the one who taught it.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who turn into a different person around bosses, angry people or anyone who leans on them, and cannot seem to stop.
modalities.cautions: Ambassadors were usually first posted in family relationships, so a licensed clinician with training in trauma care and parts work leads, and people with dissociative conditions need specialist care rather than more inner figures. Naming the first posting uses only memories you already have, any sense of who taught the ambassador is impression rather than evidence of what happened, and the work is never turned into a hunt for forgotten events, so if no first posting comes to mind it stays with present-day people; it is untested and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Turn into someone else around bosses or angry people? Inner Ambassadors is a new idea: with a therapist, show the side of you that learned its job with one person long ago how each real boss differs from that person, one dossier at a time. Untested.

modalities.name: Parts Interview You
modalities.tagline: Your wary inner sides question you before they trust you.
modalities.whatItIs: Parts Interview You is a fresh, unproven idea that reverses the usual direction of parts work and runs it as a formal, structured process. Instead of you asking a protective side about its job, the wary sides of you interview you, the adult in charge, about whether you can now be trusted with what they have guarded since long ago.
modalities.coreIdea: Protectors often learned early that the adults around them could not cope, so they may doubt the adult you as well, and a formal chance to question you might build trust on their terms.
modalities.whatYouDo: The therapist helps a protective side of you write a short list of questions, such as 'what will you do if the old fear comes back', and you answer each one in session while the side listens. It rates its trust after each answer and says what would raise it, and the interview resumes every few weeks with new questions.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults whose protective habits refuse to budge and who suspect part of them simply does not trust them yet.
modalities.cautions: Hard questions from wary sides can stir up shame and old pain, so the lead must be a licensed, trauma-trained clinician experienced in parts work who keeps the pace gentle. The interview stays with today's answers, keeps within what you already recall, treats any image of the past as impression rather than evidence, and is never used to dig up forgotten events; with no evidence for it yet, it should not replace well-tested care.
modalities.tweet: What if your wary inner sides got to interview you before trusting you? Parts Interview You is a new concept: protective parts ask the adult you hard questions and rate their trust. For people whose habits refuse to budge. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Grievance Hour for Parts
modalities.tagline: A protected hour for your inner sides to air old complaints.
modalities.whatItIs: Grievance Hour for Parts is a new idea that turns away from wishing everyone well and lets the sides of you voice their grudges and resentments, especially the old ones some sides have carried since childhood. Nothing has to be forgiven, resolved or acted on, and the therapist simply helps each grievance be heard in full.
modalities.coreIdea: Resentments held since early life can keep sides of you stuck in an old role, so a protected space to voice them, without pressure to be kind, might let them loosen in their own time.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a loosely structured session, a therapist invites any side of you with a grievance to speak, whether toward someone in your life, toward another side of you or toward you yourself. You speak for it in the first person, staying with the grievance rather than the events behind it, and the hour ends with a short settling and a reminder that nothing said needs to be acted on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel they should always be understanding, swallow anger, or carry old resentments they are ashamed of.
modalities.cautions: Voicing old anger can stir up strong feelings and painful history, so it belongs only in sessions with a clinician experienced in IFS-style parts work and trauma care, and no grievance should be acted on during or straight after a session. Anyone at risk of harming themselves or others needs specialist help first.
modalities.tweet: Always the understanding one? Grievance Hour for Parts is a new concept: a protected hour where the sides of you air old grudges out loud, with nothing to forgive or resolve. For people who swallow their anger. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: What They Still Hope For
modalities.tagline: Hearing the old hopes your inner sides are still waiting on.
modalities.whatItIs: What They Still Hope For is a proposed practice that turns parts work toward old longing. Where insight meditation loosens attachment by watching experience come and go, this practice takes attachment seriously and asks each side of you what it has been hoping for since long ago, such as an apology, a rescue or a parent who finally understands.
modalities.coreIdea: A side of you may keep a painful pattern alive because it is still waiting for something that cannot come in the old form, so hearing the hope fully might let it choose what to do with it.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist helps you find a side of you that seems to be waiting and ask, gently, what it hopes will happen and who it is waiting for, staying with the hope itself rather than the events behind it. Over several sessions you and the side decide together whether to keep the hope, change its shape or grieve it, and nothing is decided before the side is ready.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who keep returning to the same disappointing people or situations, as if waiting for a different ending.
modalities.cautions: Old hopes are often tied to family relationships and can bring strong grief or anger, so a licensed clinician skilled in both trauma care and parts work leads, and decisions about real relationships are never rushed because of it. The work rests only on memories you already have, a side's hope is not evidence of what happened, it never goes looking for forgotten events, and it is untested.
modalities.tweet: Still waiting for an apology that never comes? What They Still Hope For is an untested concept: parts work that asks each side of you what it has hoped for since long ago, then helps it decide what to do with that hope. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: What Love Looked Like
modalities.tagline: Gently exploring what each inner side learned love looks like.
modalities.whatItIs: What Love Looked Like is a speculative idea for slow, quiet parts work that explores the picture of love each side of you learned long ago, such as love as worry, love as control, love as earning or love as keeping quiet. Sessions are calm, open and unhurried, with no exercises, and nothing is asked to change.
modalities.coreIdea: Sides of us often still recognize love only in the shape they first learned, so seeing that shape clearly, without judging it, might explain why some kinds of care feel wrong and others feel familiar.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a long, quiet settling, a therapist invites any side of you to show what love looks like to it, through a word, an image or a feeling, and simply stays with what comes. You do not go looking for the events behind it, and the session ends with a few minutes of rest and a short note of what each side showed.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find themselves drawn to the same painful kind of relationship, or who feel uneasy when love arrives in a calmer form.
modalities.cautions: Old pictures of love are tied to family relationships and can bring up grief, so a licensed therapist with training in both trauma care and parts work leads, and anyone in an unsafe relationship needs practical safety support first. What a side shows is an image, not evidence of what happened, the session keeps to what you already remember, and it is never used to hunt for forgotten events; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: Does love only feel real when it looks like worry or control? What Love Looked Like is an untested concept: slow, quiet parts work exploring the picture of love each side of you learned long ago, without judging it. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Old Self-Soothing Words
modalities.tagline: Refreshing the comforting phrases your young sides invented long ago.
modalities.whatItIs: Old Self-Soothing Words is an untested concept that works with the phrases sides of you invented long ago to get through hard moments alone, such as 'it doesn't matter', 'just keep going' or 'nobody needs to know'. In quiet, inward sessions you get to know each old phrase, honor what it once did, and ask whether the side using it would like gentler words now.
modalities.coreIdea: Children left to soothe themselves often invent phrases that worked then but hardened into rules, so refreshing the words themselves, with the side's agreement, might keep the comfort and lose the harshness.
modalities.whatYouDo: Working mostly in silence with a therapist's brief prompts, you notice a phrase that runs in your head when things get hard and ask which side of you says it and what it protected you from feeling. If the side agrees, you try out a new phrase together, such as 'this is hard and I can ask for help', and repeat it quietly at the end of each session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who comfort themselves with words that also shut them down, such as 'it's fine' or 'stop being dramatic'.
modalities.cautions: Old soothing phrases often guard painful feelings, so a licensed, trauma-trained clinician experienced in parts work leads, and no phrase is replaced before its side agrees. The work stays with the phrase as it runs today, draws only on memories you already have, takes no image of its origin as evidence of events, and never seeks forgotten ones; it is untested and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: 'It's fine. Just keep going.' Old Self-Soothing Words is a new idea: parts work with the comforting phrases young sides of you invented to cope alone, honoring what each did and letting it choose gentler words. Untested; with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Clean Endings Practice
modalities.tagline: Closing each inner conversation carefully, for sides that fear goodbyes.
modalities.whatItIs: Clean Endings Practice is a proposed form of parts work for sides of you that learned long ago that endings mean being dropped or forgotten. Instead of pushing on for as long as possible, every inner conversation is closed carefully and on time, so these sides can slowly learn that a goodbye can be safe.
modalities.coreIdea: Where old endings taught that being left is dangerous, many small, reliable, well-made endings might teach something new without any need to revisit the old ones.
modalities.whatYouDo: In calm, guided sessions, the inner work stops about 15 minutes before the end, and a therapist helps you tell each side you met what will happen next, ask whether it needs anything before you go, and picture it settling somewhere comfortable. The same short closing is repeated at the end of every session, and you note how the sides respond to it over the weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who leave sessions shaken, keep replaying them for days, or find it hard to put feelings down once they are stirred up.
modalities.cautions: Endings can stir up old feelings about abandonment, so the lead must be a licensed clinician who has trained in trauma care and in parts work. The closing ritual looks forward, works only from memories you already hold, treats any old feeling it stirs as a feeling rather than evidence of past events, and is never used to retrieve forgotten ones; it is untested and best kept alongside any care you already receive.
modalities.tweet: Leave therapy shaken and replaying it for days? Concept: Clean Endings Practice. Parts work that closes every inner conversation carefully, for sides of you that learned long ago that endings mean being dropped. Untested; with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Smallest Voice Decides
modalities.tagline: Letting your longest-silenced inner side choose the direction.
modalities.whatItIs: The Smallest Voice Decides is an experimental idea that turns the usual inner hierarchy upside down. Instead of the strongest, most capable sides of you running things, the quietest side, often one silenced long ago because its needs seemed too much for the people around it, chooses what each session is about and when it ends.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner systems are often run by protectors that formed to keep an early need quiet, so handing the lead to that silenced voice for a while might show what it has needed all along.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the start of each loosely structured session, a therapist helps you notice which side of you feels smallest or least heard and asks what it would like to do today, whether that is talking, resting or just being noticed. The more powerful sides are asked to step back and watch, and the therapist checks that they agree. The work stays with what the small side needs now, not with the events that once silenced it.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who are always capable and in control on the outside, and who sense a small, unheard part of themselves underneath.
modalities.cautions: Long-silenced sides often carry old pain and protectors may push back when sidelined, so a licensed clinician with training in trauma care and parts work leads at a gentle pace. The work stays inside what you already recall, impressions of how a side was silenced are not evidence of events, and it is never used to search out forgotten ones; it is unproven and no replacement for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: The Smallest Voice Decides. Parts work with a therapist where the quietest side of you, often one silenced long ago, chooses what each session is about while capable sides step back. For people always in control outside. Not yet tested.

modalities.name: Old Imaginary Allies
modalities.tagline: Inviting back the imaginary friends and heroes of childhood.
modalities.whatItIs: Old Imaginary Allies is a hypothetical practice that draws on childhood imagination rather than memory of events: the imaginary friends, invented heroes and story creatures many children make up for company or courage. In guided imagery these allies, or new ones of the same kind, are invited back to keep company with young sides of you that still need them.
modalities.coreIdea: Many children build imaginary allies to get through hard times, and inner creations of that kind may still be available to the sides of you that formed in that era.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist helps you bring to mind, or freshly invent, an ally of the kind a child might imagine, such as a brave talking dog or a knight who guards the bedroom door, and describe it in rich detail. You then picture the ally sitting with a young side of you and notice how that side responds, entirely within the imagination.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who had a vivid imaginative life as children, or who find it easier to accept comfort from a playful figure than from a person.
modalities.cautions: Childhood imagination can bring the hard times it helped with close, so a licensed therapist with trauma training and parts experience leads, allies stay clearly imaginary, and people with dissociative conditions or a history of psychosis need specialist care instead. You bring back an old ally only if you already remember it, or invent a new one, the ally is not evidence of what your childhood was like, and it is never turned into a hunt for forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: Remember the imaginary friend who kept you brave as a kid? Old Imaginary Allies is an untested idea: with a therapist, invented heroes and creatures of that kind are invited back to keep company with the young sides of you. For vivid imaginers.

modalities.name: Laughing With Parts
modalities.tagline: Gentle, playful humor with the sides of you, never at them.
modalities.whatItIs: Laughing With Parts is a new idea that brings lightness into parts work, which usually moves slowly and solemnly. You and a therapist find the gentle comedy in sides of you that took on very serious jobs very young, such as a worrier that has been planning for disasters since primary school, always laughing with them and never at them.
modalities.coreIdea: Many sides took on grown-up jobs while still small, and affectionate humor about how long and hard they have worked might soften old rules that solemn attention cannot shift.
modalities.whatYouDo: The therapist helps you describe one side of you in vivid, affectionate terms, including how long it has been on duty, and give it a funny name or catchphrase, checking that the side enjoys the joke. You then talk with it in that playful spirit about the old job it took on, and stop the humor at once if any side feels mocked.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with a strong sense of humor who find solemn therapy heavy, or who are very hard on their own quirks.
modalities.cautions: Humor can tip into mockery or be used to dodge real pain, so a licensed clinician skilled in both trauma care and parts work leads and watches for both. Talk about a side's old job keeps to what you already remember, treats any picture of when it started as impression rather than evidence, and never goes looking for forgotten events; it is untested and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Has your worrier been planning for disasters since primary school? Laughing With Parts is a new concept: parts work that finds the gentle comedy in sides of you that took on serious jobs very young, never laughing at them. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Separate Rooms Agreement
modalities.tagline: Two long-clashing inner sides agreeing to live apart in peace.
modalities.whatItIs: Separate Rooms Agreement is an untested concept for sides of you that have clashed since early life, often because the same old situation taught them opposite lessons, such as one learning to fight back and another learning to hide. Instead of pushing them toward teamwork, the practice helps them settle into peaceful coexistence, each with its own room, the way housemates who will never be friends can still share a home.
modalities.coreIdea: Some inner conflicts are as old as the person and may never fully resolve, so a quiet agreement to live and let live might bring more peace than pushing for harmony.
modalities.whatYouDo: Working mostly in silent inner reflection, with a therapist offering a few prompts, you picture two sides of you that have long clashed and ask each what room it needs and what it wants the other to stop doing. You settle on simple written house rules, such as 'the fighter does not mock the hider', and review them every few weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults worn out by an inner conflict they have had for as long as they can remember, who would settle for peace instead of agreement.
modalities.cautions: Keeping sides apart must never mean ignoring a side in distress, so a licensed, trauma-trained clinician experienced in parts work leads and checks that no part is shut away, and people with dissociative conditions need specialist care instead. The house rules are written for today from memories you already have, a long clash is not evidence of particular events, and the work is never used to dig up forgotten ones; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Separate Rooms Agreement. For two sides of you that have clashed since childhood, like the fighter and the hider, therapist-led parts work that helps them live apart in peace with simple house rules. For people tired of an inner war. Untested.

modalities.name: Debts That Were Never Yours
modalities.tagline: Reviewing the old debts your inner sides believe they owe.
modalities.whatItIs: Debts That Were Never Yours is an invented practice that works with one kind of old learning: responsibilities a child took on that were never theirs, such as keeping a parent happy, holding the family together or making up for someone else's sadness. In a structured, case-by-case review, sides of you that still carry these debts set them out one by one, and each is examined and then kept, reduced or cancelled by agreement.
modalities.coreIdea: Sides of you may still be paying debts they took on as children, and a formal, orderly review might let them stop paying the ones that were never theirs to owe.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist helps a side of you name one debt and its terms, for example 'I must never make anyone worry', and asks what it believes it owes and what it fears would happen if payment stopped, staying with the debt as a belief rather than with the events or people behind it. You record the debt, the side's decision and any conditions, and return to the record every few weeks to see how the side is doing without that payment.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel responsible for everyone's feelings, or who grew up looking after the adults around them.
modalities.cautions: Looking at what you carried as a child can bring up grief and anger toward family, so the lead must be a licensed clinician who has trained in trauma care and in parts work, and real duties you have today, such as caring for someone, need practical support and are never dropped on impulse. Any sense of how a debt began is an impression rather than evidence, the review works only from memories you already hold, and it is never used to hunt for forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: Still paying debts you took on as a kid, like keeping a parent happy? Debts That Were Never Yours is a new concept: therapist-led parts work that reviews each old debt one by one and lets your inner sides stop paying the ones never theirs. Untested.

modalities.name: Inner Casting Call
modalities.tagline: Casting each inner side as a character from its era's stories.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Casting Call is an experimental idea that gives each side of you a character to play, chosen from the stories of the years when that side first formed, such as the books, cartoons or films of your childhood. Instead of attending to raw sensation, you and a therapist work through story, using those old characters to understand how each side learned to act.
modalities.coreIdea: The stories we absorbed as children often gave us our first models of how to be, so casting a side with a familiar character might shed light on its style and on what new role it could grow into.
modalities.whatYouDo: In each session you describe one side of you and try out characters from stories you already remember, often ones from around the age that side seems to be, until one feels right. You talk with the therapist about what that character did at its best and worst, imagine how it would handle a current situation differently, and may recast the side as it changes.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who love stories and find it easier to understand themselves through characters.
modalities.cautions: Old stories can bring the years they come from close, and fictional labels can make a side seem more fixed than it is, so the tone stays playful and a licensed therapist trained in trauma care and parts work leads; people with dissociative conditions need specialist care instead. You cast only from stories you already remember, the casting is play rather than evidence of what happened at that age, and it is never used to retrieve forgotten events or years; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: Who would play your inner critic? Inner Casting Call is an untested idea: with a therapist you cast each side of you as a character from the stories you loved when that side formed, a cartoon hero or a fairy-tale villain, and learn from them.

modalities.name: The Old Lucky Rules
modalities.tagline: Meeting the small rituals your inner sides still keep for luck.
modalities.whatItIs: The Old Lucky Rules is a proposed practice for quiet, steady parts work with the small private rules sides of you adopted long ago because they seemed to keep bad things away, such as worrying in advance, never celebrating too early or always saying goodbye properly. Instead of breaking the rules, you get to know the side that keeps each one and what it has been guarding against.
modalities.coreIdea: Many such rules began as a child's way of feeling some control in a frightening world, so understanding that old bargain might let a side decide, in its own time, which rules it still needs.
modalities.whatYouDo: In calm sessions with a therapist, you list the small rules you follow without quite believing in them, choose one, and ask the side behind it what it believes the rule prevents and what it would need to relax its grip. Nothing is dropped suddenly; any change is a small, agreed loosening that you check on in later sessions.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who keep little rituals or worries going just in case, and who sense these started long ago.
modalities.cautions: Rituals that take up a lot of time or cause distress may be OCD, which needs specialist treatment rather than this practice, and the work is led only by a licensed, trauma-trained clinician experienced in parts work. It stays with the rule as you follow it now, keeps within what you already recall, treats any idea of where the rule began as impression rather than evidence, and is never used to search out forgotten events; it is untested and not a stand-in for tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Never celebrate too early, always worry in advance, just in case? The Old Lucky Rules is an untested idea: quiet parts work with the small rules young sides of you adopted to keep bad things away. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Habit Prototype Week
modalities.tagline: Trying five quick versions of a new habit, then keeping one.
modalities.whatItIs: Habit Prototype Week is an untested concept that borrows rapid prototyping from product design and applies it to everyday change, with no imagery and no look back at the past. Instead of committing to one carefully planned new habit, you try five rough versions of it in real life, one a day, then keep the one that fit best.
modalities.coreIdea: A first plan for change is rarely the right one, so testing several quick, cheap versions out in the world might find a workable habit faster than perfecting one on paper.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach, you choose a habit you want, such as keeping in touch with friends, and sketch five very different versions, from a two-line message each morning to a standing Sunday phone call. You try one version each weekday, give it a quick score for ease and enjoyment, and at a short check-in pick a winner to run for the next month.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who stall because they want the perfect plan before starting, or who have abandoned many carefully designed routines.
modalities.cautions: Keep every version small, cheap and safe, and drop any version that leaves you more stressed than before. If low mood makes even tiny habits impossible, that calls for a clinician rather than more experiments.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Habit Prototype Week. Instead of planning one perfect new habit, try five rough versions in real life, one a day, score each, and keep the one that fits. For people who stall waiting for the perfect plan. Untested; keep versions small.

modalities.name: Calm-Day Constitution
modalities.tagline: Rules you write when calm, to guide you when you are not.
modalities.whatItIs: Calm-Day Constitution is a speculative idea that takes the structure of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward self-governance. Rather than hearing out the different sides of you that pull each way, you act as one lawmaker: on a calm day you write a short constitution of standing decisions for heated moments, and it can only be amended by a set procedure.
modalities.coreIdea: Decisions made in distress are often the ones we regret, so the practice lets your calm self set guidelines in advance and makes changing them slow on purpose.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach or therapist, you draft about ten articles, such as 'I never send an angry message until the next morning' or 'I do not quit a job in the same week I want to'. When a heated moment comes you follow the article, and any change must be written down, wait a week and be agreed in a session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who act on impulse in heated moments and later regret it, and who like clear commitments.
