modalities.cautions: Articles must stay kind and flexible enough for real emergencies, and they should never stop you from seeking help or leaving an unsafe situation. Strong impulsivity linked to mood swings, substance use or self-harm needs a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: What if your calm self could write rules for your stressed self? Calm-Day Constitution is a new idea: write ten standing decisions on a good day, follow them in heated moments, and amend them only after a week's wait. For impulsive regretters. Untested.

modalities.name: Tolerance Specs
modalities.tagline: Writing each standard as an acceptable range, not a perfect point.
modalities.whatItIs: Tolerance Specs is a speculative idea that borrows tolerances from engineering, where a part is fine anywhere within a stated range, and applies them to personal standards. Instead of simply accepting whatever happens or chasing an ideal, you write precise specs with an acceptable band for the things you judge yourself on, and you count both too little and too much effort as out of spec.
modalities.coreIdea: Perfectionism sets every standard as a single point that can only be missed, so a two-sided range might make good enough precise and make overwork count as a miss too.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist, you pick three areas, such as work reports, tidiness and replies to messages, and write a spec for each, for example 'a report is in spec if it covers the brief, has been checked once and took under three hours'. For a few weeks you note whether each piece of work landed in spec, under or over, and adjust the specs in session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with perfectionist standards who also overwork, and who like clear, measurable rules.
modalities.cautions: Specs should be kind, and for some people writing rules can become another form of control, so the therapist watches for this. Perfectionism tied to disordered eating, severe anxiety or depression needs a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: What if 'good enough' had a precise spec? Tolerance Specs is a new idea: write each personal standard as an acceptable range, the way an engineer would, and count overwork as out of spec too. For perfectionists who never stop. No evidence yet.

modalities.name: Day Zero Mornings
modalities.tagline: Planning each day as if your history did not decide it.
modalities.whatItIs: Day Zero Mornings is an experimental idea that takes CBT's focus on the present to its limit and sets aside every question of where a problem came from. Each morning you plan the day with a short checklist that rules out reasons from the past, such as 'I always fail at this', and asks only what you would choose to do today if you were starting fresh.
modalities.coreIdea: Stories about who we have always been can quietly decide each day for us, so a structured daily fresh start might loosen that momentum.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every morning for five minutes you answer the same four written questions, such as 'what would a fresh-start version of me do first today', and pick one action. In the evening you note only how today went, without comparing it to the past, and every week or two you review the notebook with a coach.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel trapped by their track record, or who keep repeating patterns because 'that is just who I am'.
modalities.cautions: This is a daily exercise, not a way to ignore real history: past trauma, debts or health problems still need proper attention. If old memories keep pushing in, that is a sign to work with a clinician rather than to push harder.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Day Zero Mornings. Each morning a five-minute checklist asks what you'd do today if your history didn't decide it, with no 'I always fail at this' allowed. For people who feel trapped by their track record.

modalities.name: Teacher's Turn
modalities.tagline: Learning thinking skills by preparing to teach them to others.
modalities.whatItIs: Teacher's Turn is a proposed, untested group format in which the skills of CBT are learned by teaching them, entirely through talk. In a small facilitated group, members take turns preparing and teaching one practical thinking skill to the others, using examples from their own lives that they choose to share.
modalities.coreIdea: People often understand and remember a skill best when they have to explain it to someone else, so the practice turns every member into a teacher.
modalities.whatYouDo: Groups of five to seven meet weekly for 90 minutes, and each week one or two members give a ten-minute lesson on a skill the facilitator assigned, such as spotting all-or-nothing thinking. The others ask questions until the lesson is clear, the teacher writes a one-page handout from the discussion, and members keep a growing binder of handouts written by each other.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who learn best by explaining, enjoy helping others, or feel more confident in a teaching role.
modalities.cautions: Teaching in front of a group can feel exposing, so lessons are short, feedback rules are strict and anyone can pass, and the facilitator should be a trained clinician. People in crisis or with severe social anxiety may need individual support first.
modalities.tweet: Best way to learn something? Teach it. Teacher's Turn is a new concept: in a small group, members take turns giving ten-minute lessons on a thinking skill and writing handouts for each other. For people who learn by explaining. Still to be tested.

modalities.name: Second-Draft Thinking
modalities.tagline: Recording your thinking, editing it, then thinking it through again.
modalities.whatItIs: Second-Draft Thinking is a prototype idea that handles a train of thought like a piece of writing that can be drafted and revised. Rather than waiting for a vague bodily sense to become clear, you record yourself thinking aloud about a problem, edit the transcript with a therapist into a clearer second draft, and then think the problem through aloud again.
modalities.coreIdea: Thinking may improve with drafts the way writing does, so editing a record of your own thinking and rethinking from the edit might leave a clearer, kinder version you can return to.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you record five minutes of thinking aloud about something on your mind and turn it into text with a transcription app. In session you and the therapist cut repetition, mark claims you never checked and add the questions you skipped, then you record a second take from the edited page, compare the two and keep the better draft.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who overthink in circles, like writing and editing, and want a concrete way to think a problem through more clearly.
modalities.cautions: Reading your own worries in print can be uncomfortable or feed self-criticism, so the therapist keeps the tone curious and kind. Keep recordings private and stored securely, and get a full assessment if worry is constant or overwhelming.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: Second-Draft Thinking. Record five minutes of thinking aloud, edit the transcript with a therapist the way a writer revises a draft, then think it through again from the edit. For people who overthink in circles. Untested.

modalities.name: Skill Belt Grading
modalities.tagline: Earning colored belts in practical mental skills, like a martial art.
modalities.whatItIs: Skill Belt Grading is a speculative idea that arranges the practical skills of CBT into graded levels, in place of open-ended personal unfolding. Skills from noticing a thought to planning a hard conversation are grouped into belts like a martial art, each with a short practical test.
modalities.coreIdea: Visible stages and earned milestones may keep people practicing skills that otherwise fade, and turn progress into something you can see.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach, you start at the first belt, which might cover noticing and naming feelings, and practice its three skills for a few weeks. To pass, you show each skill in a short live test, such as calming yourself after a stressful role-play, and then move on to the next belt.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who like goals, levels and clear progress, and who lose motivation when improvement feels invisible.
modalities.cautions: Grading can feed perfectionism or shame, so failing a test only means practicing longer, and belts are never compared between people. Low motivation can be a sign of depression, which needs proper assessment and care rather than more tests.
modalities.tweet: Mental skills, graded like a martial art. Skill Belt Grading is an untested idea: earn belts in practical skills, from naming feelings to handling hard talks, each with a short live test. For people who lose motivation when progress feels invisible.

modalities.name: Sixty-Second Decisions
modalities.tagline: Timed group drills in making small decisions quickly and sticking to them.
modalities.whatItIs: Sixty-Second Decisions is an untested concept that makes decisiveness itself the skill, practiced under a facilitator's tight control. In a small group, members make many real but low-stakes decisions against a one-minute timer, such as which of two tasks to start or what to cook tonight, and then stick to them.
modalities.coreIdea: Overthinking small choices can drain whole days, so repeated, timed practice in deciding quickly and living with the result might make decisiveness feel familiar.
modalities.whatYouDo: Groups of five or six meet weekly, and each member brings a list of ten small pending decisions from their own life. The facilitator calls each one, the member decides out loud within sixty seconds, and at the next meeting everyone reports how the decisions turned out and how much the outcome actually mattered.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who agonize over small choices, check endlessly before deciding, or lose evenings to indecision.
modalities.cautions: Only small, reversible decisions belong in the drill; anything about money, health, relationships or safety is left out. Indecision driven by OCD, depression or severe anxiety needs a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: Lose whole evenings deciding what to cook? Sixty-Second Decisions is a new concept: in a small facilitated group you make ten small real decisions, sixty seconds each, then report how little the outcome mattered. Untested; small choices only.

modalities.name: Routine Swap
modalities.tagline: Trading one daily routine with another person for a week.
modalities.whatItIs: Routine Swap is a proposed practice that replaces wishing others well with a concrete exchange. Members of a small group pair up and, for one week, each tries out one of the other's everyday routines, such as how they start the morning, clear the inbox or wind down at night, then compares notes on what it showed them about their own habits and assumptions.
modalities.coreIdea: Our own routines can feel like the only way to live, so borrowing someone else's for a week might reveal which of our assumptions are rules and which are just habits.
modalities.whatYouDo: Groups of four to six meet weekly; each person describes one routine in exact steps, and a facilitator pairs people whose routines differ. During the week you follow your partner's routine as written and note what thoughts come up, such as 'this is lazy' or 'I could never', and at the next meeting both partners report back.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel stuck in their own way of doing things, or who suspect other people simply live differently.
modalities.cautions: Swapped routines must be safe and ordinary, with nothing involving medication, diet changes, driving or physical risk, and anyone can decline a pairing. People in crisis need individual professional help rather than a group.
modalities.tweet: Ever wondered how other people actually start their mornings? Routine Swap is an untested idea: in a small group, trade one everyday routine with a partner for a week and notice what your own habits assume. For people stuck in one way of living.

modalities.name: The Believer Test
modalities.tagline: Writing a hopeful view so convincingly no one can tell.
modalities.whatItIs: The Believer Test is an untested concept that borrows a debating game, in which you try to state a view so well that listeners cannot tell whether you really hold it, and turns it on your own gloomiest conclusions. Rather than quietly noting thoughts as they pass, members of a small group each write a short case for a kinder view of their own situation, written as if they fully believed it.
modalities.coreIdea: A hopeful view you cannot even state convincingly stays foreign, so practicing until you can argue it like a true believer might make it a real option for thinking, before you agree with it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week the facilitator collects one conclusion from each member, such as 'my friends only put up with me', and each member writes a 150-word case for a kinder reading of their own situation in the voice of someone who believes it. The group reads the cases without names and rates how convincing each sounds, and you rewrite yours until it reads as if a believer wrote it, then note whether your own view moved at all.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who can list every reason things are bad but cannot put the hopeful case into words.
modalities.cautions: Writing a view you do not hold can feel fake at first, so no one is pushed to adopt it, and the ratings judge only how convincing the writing sounds, never you or your situation, so a low score just means another rewrite. In a group this small people may guess who wrote what, so share only conclusions you would be at ease having recognized; the facilitator is a trained clinician, and anyone in crisis should get one-to-one care first.
modalities.tweet: New concept: The Believer Test. In a small group, you write the hopeful case about your own situation as if you fully believed it, others rate it blind, and you rewrite until it convinces. For people who can't put the hopeful view into words. Not yet tested.

modalities.name: Season Review Sessions
modalities.tagline: Long, calm sessions every three months to see slow patterns.
modalities.whatItIs: Season Review Sessions is an experimental idea that slows CBT right down, trading short, intense bursts for long, rare reviews. Instead of weekly sessions, you meet a therapist once every three months for a long, calm, structured review of the whole season, looking for patterns that only show over months.
modalities.coreIdea: Some thinking habits move too slowly to notice week to week, so stepping back to a seasonal timescale might reveal them clearly.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before each review you fill in a simple monthly sheet on mood, sleep, stress and key events, and the three-hour session starts with a few quiet minutes, then lays the months out on a timeline. Together you mark recurring dips and recoveries, name the thoughts that came with them and set one small aim for the next season.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with slow, recurring patterns, such as winter lows or yearly work crunches, or who cannot attend weekly therapy.
modalities.cautions: Three months is a long gap, so you need a clear plan for getting help sooner if things worsen, and it is not suitable during a crisis. Seasonal low mood that is severe deserves a medical assessment.
modalities.tweet: Some patterns only show over months. Season Review Sessions is a new idea: one long, calm session every three months to lay the season out on a timeline and spot slow cycles, like winter lows. For people who can't do weekly therapy. No evidence yet.

modalities.name: The Passed Notepad
modalities.tagline: Working through a problem alone, one passed written question at a time.
modalities.whatItIs: The Passed Notepad is an untested concept in which you work through a problem alone and in writing, in a quiet room, while a therapist next door passes in one short written question at a time. With no conversation, no tone of voice and no pressure to answer fast, the session is quiet, slow and private, almost entirely your own time.
modalities.coreIdea: Spoken conversation can rush people, and taking the voice out of the room might leave space for slower, more careful thinking.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session opens with one written question about your week on the desk, and for about forty minutes you answer alone, in your own time, passing the page out whenever you want the next question. At the end you keep the pages, mark one line you want to remember and write one small next step on the last page.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who freeze in spoken conversation, say what they think others want to hear, or think best with a pen.
modalities.cautions: Writing is slower, so this format is not suitable in a crisis, and the therapist should check in aloud if your notes suggest you are struggling. Keep the pages somewhere private.
modalities.tweet: Freeze up when you have to talk about yourself? The Passed Notepad is a new idea: you work through a problem alone in a quiet room, answering short questions a therapist passes in, no speaking. For people who think best with a pen. Untested.

modalities.name: Done in the Room
modalities.tagline: All the practice happens live, with no homework at all.
modalities.whatItIs: Done in the Room proposes removing homework from CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) and doing all the practice together with the therapist during sessions. Where most CBT asks you to practice alone between visits, here the therapist leads every exercise live, step by step, so nothing depends on stamina or willpower at home.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people cannot keep up practice alone, so moving all of it into longer guided sessions might make the method usable for them.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sessions last about two hours, once or twice a week, and each one includes a full practice block led by the therapist, such as filling in a worksheet together or making a hard phone call while the therapist sits beside you. You leave with no tasks, only a short summary of what you did.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who have dropped out of therapy because of homework, live in chaotic circumstances, or find it hard to get started on their own.
modalities.cautions: Longer sessions can be tiring and costly, and some skills may fade without practice at home, so progress in this untested format should be reviewed regularly. Severe depression or suicidal thoughts call for prompt professional help.
modalities.tweet: Hated therapy homework? Concept: Done in the Room. All the practice happens live in longer sessions with your therapist, from worksheets to that dreaded phone call, so nothing depends on willpower at home. For people who can't self-start. Untested so far.

modalities.name: Subtraction Weeks
modalities.tagline: Removing one obligation a week instead of trying harder.
modalities.whatItIs: Subtraction Weeks is a speculative, untested idea that takes CBT in the direction of lightening the load rather than building more strength to carry it. Each week, with a therapist's help, you list your commitments, weigh what each costs and gives, and remove or shrink exactly one.
modalities.coreIdea: Stress often comes from the sheer number of demands rather than a lack of coping skills, so steady subtraction might do more than another self-improvement plan.
modalities.whatYouDo: In the first session you write down every regular commitment, from work duties to group chats and favors, and score each for energy cost and value. Each week you pick one to drop, delegate or shrink, predict what will happen, and report back on what actually did.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel overloaded and keep adding coping strategies instead of reducing demands.
modalities.cautions: Some duties, such as caring for children or legal obligations, cannot simply be dropped, so subtraction focuses on what is truly optional. Overload with exhaustion or low mood may also need medical care.
modalities.tweet: Overloaded? Instead of trying harder, Subtraction Weeks is a new idea: each week, with a therapist, you weigh your commitments and drop or shrink exactly one, then see what really happens. For people who keep adding instead of removing. Not yet tested.

modalities.name: Second Language Thinking
modalities.tagline: Thinking through worries in a language you are still learning.
modalities.whatItIs: Second Language Thinking is an experimental idea that uses a foreign language you are learning as a tool for distance rather than seeking comfort. Research on decision-making suggests people often reason less emotionally in a second language, though it has been studied in decision tasks rather than in worry, so you write and think through recurring worries in that language, slowly and with simple words.
modalities.coreIdea: A worry spelled out in plain, effortful learner's words may lose some of its heat, making it easier to see what it actually claims.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach, you pick one recurring worry and write it in your learning language in short, simple sentences, using a dictionary where needed, then answer it in the same language. Most of the practice happens on your own a few times a week, and every week or two you bring the pages to a session to see how the worries read.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults learning a language who overthink in their first one, or who enjoy language puzzles.
modalities.cautions: A learner's language can feel clumsy and frustrating, so keep it light, and switch back to your first language for anything urgent or serious. Persistent worry or low mood needs a full assessment by a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Second Language Thinking. Write your recurring worries in a language you're learning, in simple words, and answer them in it too; decision research hints people may reason less emotionally in a second language. For learners who overthink.

modalities.name: Good Loser Games
modalities.tagline: Practicing losing well in low-stakes games against stronger players.
modalities.whatItIs: Good Loser Games is a new idea that turns losing into a skill practiced on purpose, in brisk, competitive games rather than calm, flowing movement. In a facilitated group, members play quick board or card games against stronger opponents, expect to lose, and use each loss as practice in noticing and answering the thoughts it sets off.
modalities.coreIdea: Fear of failing often comes down to what we tell ourselves after a loss, and losing often, in games where nothing is at stake, might make those thoughts familiar and easier to answer.
modalities.whatYouDo: Groups of four to six meet weekly for 90 minutes and play short games, such as fast chess or a card game, each paired against someone better. After each loss you write down the first thought that came, such as 'I'm hopeless', and one fairer reply, and the facilitator closes with a short round on what losing felt like.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who avoid anything they might not be good at, or who take every loss as proof about themselves.
modalities.cautions: Games can become heated, so the facilitator keeps them friendly and anyone can sit out a round. Strong feelings of worthlessness after setbacks may be a sign of depression that needs a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Hate losing? Good Loser Games is an untested concept: a small group plays fast board and card games against stronger players on purpose, and practices answering the thoughts each loss sets off. For people who avoid anything they might fail at.

modalities.name: Your Thought Taxonomy
modalities.tagline: Sorting your own thoughts into categories you invent yourself.
modalities.whatItIs: Your Thought Taxonomy is a speculative idea that has you sort your own recurring thoughts the way a naturalist sorts specimens, into categories you invent rather than a standard list of thinking errors. Working silently in session, with a therapist beside you guiding every step, you build a small personal field guide to the kinds of thought your mind produces.
modalities.coreIdea: Naming a thought's kind can make it feel like one more specimen rather than the truth, and categories you invent yourself may fit better than any textbook list.
modalities.whatYouDo: In each session you write recent recurring thoughts on index cards and silently sort the pile into groups that feel alike, giving each group a name of your own, such as 'midnight accountant' or 'the doom forecast'. The therapist guides each sorting round and helps you refine the groups, and over the weeks you get quicker at naming which kind of thought has turned up.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who like sorting, collecting and naming things, and who prefer to work quietly.
modalities.cautions: Sorting thoughts can become another way to dwell on them, so keep the practice short and stop if it increases worry. Thoughts of self-harm should never be filed away; they need prompt professional help.
modalities.tweet: Your mind has species of thought. Your Thought Taxonomy is a new idea: sort recurring thoughts on index cards into groups you invent and name, like 'midnight accountant', and build your own field guide. For quiet collectors and sorters. Untested.

modalities.name: Image-to-Words Switching
modalities.tagline: Switching a worry between pictures and plain words, on purpose.
modalities.whatItIs: Image-to-Words Switching is a hypothetical, untested practice built on research suggesting that imagined pictures stir stronger feelings than the same thoughts put into words. Indoors and with a therapist guiding each step, you practice shifting a recurring worry from vivid mental images into plain verbal statements and back again, learning which form inflames it and which settles it.
modalities.coreIdea: Worries arrive in different forms, and finding out in session which form makes a worry flare and which steadies it, while learning to make helpful thoughts as vivid as the worries, might give you more say over which thoughts carry the most feeling day to day.
modalities.whatYouDo: The therapist asks you to describe a worry as the picture it usually comes as and rate how strong it feels, then restate it as one flat sentence and rate it again. Over several sessions you practice the switch faster, and in the other direction for helpful thoughts, which you turn into vivid images. The worry switch stays in the therapy room, where the therapist can check it is not becoming a way to dodge a feeling, while the other direction, picturing a helpful thought as vividly as a worry, is yours to practice for a few minutes a day at home.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults whose worries play like vivid movies, and who are comfortable working with imagination.
modalities.cautions: Picturing worries raises feelings for a while, and in CBT's own model turning worry into words can become a way of avoiding the feeling, which keeps worry going, so the worry switch is practiced only in session, in both directions, and never used to dodge a feeling for long. Traumatic memories belong with trauma-focused care, and strong or constant anxiety needs a fuller plan with a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Does your worry play like a movie? Image-to-Words Switching is a new concept: with a therapist, practice turning a vivid worry picture into one flat sentence, rating how strong each feels, and back again for helpful thoughts. Still to be tested.

modalities.name: Reasoning Toolkit Seminar
modalities.tagline: Reasoning tools from economics and statistics, applied to your worries.
modalities.whatItIs: Reasoning Toolkit Seminar is a proposed group practice that imports named tools of reasoning from economics and statistics, such as regression to the mean, survivorship bias and sunk costs, and applies them to personal worries and decisions. Far from raw sensory experience, it is abstract and brisk, run more like a seminar than a support group. Weekly clinical groups such as Metacognitive Training already take one thinking bias per session and apply it to members' own lives; what differs here is the source of the tools, which come from how economists and statisticians check a conclusion rather than from a clinical list of biases, and each one is turned into a pocket card with a single test question.
modalities.coreIdea: Many painful conclusions rest on reasoning slips that thinkers in other fields have already named, so learning those tools might give people fresh ways to check their own conclusions.
modalities.whatYouDo: A small group meets weekly with a trained facilitator, who introduces one tool with everyday examples, such as how an unusually bad week is often followed by a more ordinary one. Members then test the tool against one of their own conclusions in pairs, and each person leaves with that tool's card and its test question, such as 'am I judging from an extreme week?', to try during the week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who enjoy ideas, logic and puzzles, and who distrust advice that feels like positive thinking.
modalities.cautions: Clever reasoning can be used to argue away real problems, so the facilitator keeps the focus on fair checking rather than winning, and members can pass. A seminar is the wrong setting for a crisis, which calls for one-to-one care from a clinician first.
modalities.tweet: What do sunk costs and regression to the mean have to do with your worries? Reasoning Toolkit Seminar is an untested idea: a small group learns reasoning tools from economics and statistics and tests them on their own conclusions.

modalities.name: One-Sentence Apologies
modalities.tagline: Learning to apologize once, clearly and in proportion.
modalities.whatItIs: One-Sentence Apologies is a new idea that turns the exactness of CBT toward one everyday habit: apologizing too much, too long or for things that are not your fault. Moving away from emotional expression and toward measured precision, you practice reducing each apology to a single clear sentence that matches the size of what actually happened.
modalities.coreIdea: Over-apologizing can keep alive a belief that you are always in the wrong, so apologies sized exactly might help that belief shrink to fit the facts.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist, you collect apologies you have recently made or are about to make, in messages or conversation, and for each one decide whether an apology is owed at all and, if so, cut it to one sentence. Between sessions you send the trimmed versions in real life, note what you feared would happen and what did, and bring the results back.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who say sorry constantly, apologize for taking up space, or write long apologies for small things.
modalities.cautions: Some situations really do call for a full apology, so the aim is proportion, not avoiding responsibility. Constant guilt or a sense of being bad may be tied to depression or past trauma and deserves a clinician's help.
modalities.tweet: Sorry, sorry, so sorry? One-Sentence Apologies is an untested concept: with a therapist you decide whether each apology is owed and trim it to one clear sentence sized to what happened. For people who apologize for taking up space.
